doc.title: Scott Yanow interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, October 22, 2021

title: Discovering Dixieland, swing, bebop and Coltrane in college
summary: Yanow found Dixieland on radio in 1970, then swing, then Charlie Parker, Dolphy, Monk and Coltrane at college; Rowe shares his own first Coltrane record.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: I was reading about from your website your experience of going to college with LPs and I really related to that. And your description, it was quite a leap you made in a short amount of time from Pete Fountain to John Coltrane and Pharoah Sanders. Can you remember how that music affected you, expanding your listening palate back then?

Remember this is like [gap]. 1970 is when I first discovered Dixieland, it was a local radio show, and I noticed in the Los Angeles Times it mentioned it, it was like 5 to 6 PM on an FM station, Monday through Friday. So I thought well this is happy music, I’ll see what this is like. And it took a couple of days and then I was addicted to that. And then about six months later I discovered Chuck Cecil’s Swingin’ Years and I got into the Swing Era. But when I went to college all I listened to basically was Dixieland and swing for the first month or two. And I happened to be in a dormitory where there were a lot of musicians and they looked at my records, I had 25 records and they’d say, “Oh, what a huge collection.” You know they thought 25 was huge, of LPs, and they’d look through it and see Dixieland and Al Hirt and Pete Fountain. And they thought I was crazy of course. Worth remembering is Charlie Parker and Dizzy Gillespie, and I didn’t know anything about them at all so I went to a used record store and for $1.99 I saw a Charlie Parker record that had a lot of unfamiliar tunes like “Night in Tunisia” and “Groovin’ High.” But it did have one song I’d heard of called “White Christmas.” And I said, “I’ve heard this one” because there was a request for it on the radio broadcasting it. So I listened to that each day three or four times, it took me a little while to get into it. But by the end of the week the doors were open. And then I was just very curious about all other eras of jazz. So very quickly I went through and I loved Eric Dolphy and I got into Thelonious Monk and within a few months I was into John Coltrane, not just his early stuff but the latest screaming things he did with Pharoah Sanders and that’s when the musicians I knew were sure that I was crazy [gap].

It’s so interesting you say that because I shouldn’t talk about myself but very briefly I went out to get my first John Coltrane record because someone said, “You should listen to him.” And I picked up “Om.” And that was not a great place to start for me, and I’m afraid it scared me off for quite a while.
